Cancer Diagnosis via Unsupervised Learning

Pratik Kothari

2025-12-10

1. Introduction

Michigan Medicine is piloting a very expensive cancer treatment. Because each clinical trial slot is costly, the goal is not to identify all cancer patients, but instead to avoid inviting patients who do not actually have cancer.

Formally, our primary metric is Precision:

\[ \text{Precision} = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{All Patients Flagged as Positive}}. \]

  • True Positive (TP): Patient truly has cancer and is predicted as high-risk.
  • False Positive (FP): Patient is predicted as high-risk but is actually benign.

We accept that we might miss some true cancer patients (lower sensitivity/recall) as long as the ones we do invite are very likely to have cancer. However, operationally, the trial still needs enough participants, so our models should identify at least 7 true cancer patients in this dataset.

This report uses unsupervised learning to support trial selection. The labels (Cancer vs Benign) are used only at the end to evaluate our models.

We address the client’s questions as follows:

  • Q1 – PCA: Use Principal Component Analysis to reduce dimensionality, choosing between 90%, 95%, or 97% explained variance. Create a PCA dataset and justify the choice.
  • Q2 – Outlier Detection: Build at least one outlier detection model (we use kNN outlier detection and Isolation Forest) and explain parameter choices.
  • Q3 – Clustering: Build at least one clustering model (we use k-means) to test whether clustering can help diagnose cancer incidence.
  • Q4 – Increasing Precision: Combine methods and adjust thresholds to maximize precision while still finding at least 7 true cancer patients.

Throughout, we will explicitly explain our assumptions and design choices in business-friendly language.

2.1. Load Packages

# kNN-based outlier detection utilities
library(dbscan)

# Isolation Forest implementation

library(isotree)

# For PCA and scree plots (base + ggplot)
# (we'll use base prcomp + ggplot)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

3. Data Preparation & PCA (Q1)

3.1. Scaling Data

Both PCA and distance-based methods (kNN outlier, k-means) are sensitive to variable scale. A variable measured in larger units could dominate others if we do not standardize.

We therefore:

  1. Select only the numeric predictor columns (those starting with "X").
  2. Use lapply() to apply scale() to every column (mean 0, standard deviation 1).
  3. Keep this scaled matrix for PCA and all subsequent methods.
# Select only numeric predictors (assumes they're named X1, X2, ...)
X <- wbc %>% 
  select(starts_with("X"))

All X* columns are continuous or at least numeric and suitable for scaling. If there were categorical features, we would treat them separately (e.g., one-hot encoding). The WBC-style dataset is typically all numeric predictors, so this is reasonable.

3.2. Run PCA on Scaled Data

We now perform PCA on the scaled features. We use prcomp() and then examine the cumulative proportion of variance explained to decide how many PCs to keep.

set.seed(123)

pca_full <- prcomp(X_scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)

pca_summary <- summary(pca_full)

# Variance explained
var_explained <- pca_summary$importance["Proportion of Variance", ]
cumvar_explained <- pca_summary$importance["Cumulative Proportion", ]

head(cbind(Var = var_explained, CumVar = cumvar_explained), 15)
##          Var  CumVar
## PC1  0.37592 0.37592
## PC2  0.22646 0.60238
## PC3  0.09644 0.69883
## PC4  0.07332 0.77215
## PC5  0.06776 0.83990
## PC6  0.04024 0.88014
## PC7  0.02483 0.90498
## PC8  0.01600 0.92098
## PC9  0.01464 0.93561

## PC11 0.01080 0.96013
## PC12 0.00994 0.97007
## PC13 0.00686 0.97693

We can also visualize the cumulative variance to see how quickly it grows with more PCs:

pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC = 1:length(cumvar_explained),
  CumVar = cumvar_explained
)

ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC, y = CumVar)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.90, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.97, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative Proportion of Variance Explained by PCs",
    x = "Number of Principal Components",
    y = "Cumulative Variance Explained"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

3.3. Choose 90%, 95%, or 97% Variance

We were explicitly asked to choose between capturing 90%, 95%, or 97% of the variance.

We can programmatically find how many PCs are needed for each threshold:

thresholds <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.97)

pcs_needed <- sapply(thresholds, function(t) {
  which(cumvar_explained >= t)[1]
})

pcs_needed
##  PC7 PC11 PC12 
##    7   11   12

Example interpretation (your exact numbers will appear in the table above):

  • To capture 90% of the variance, we need around 7 PCs.
  • To capture 95% of the variance, we need around 11 PCs.
  • To capture 97% of the variance, we need around 12 PCs.

Choice and Rationale

  • 90% (fewer PCs) gives a strong reduction (from 30 original features down to ~7 PCs) but may discard clinically relevant variation.
  • 97% (more PCs) is closer to the full dataset but offers less simplification and may retain noise.
  • 95% is a common compromise in applied work: it keeps most of the signal while still reducing noise and dimensionality substantially.

Given that we:

  • Want stable unsupervised models (outlier detection and clustering),
  • Are not severely constrained by computational cost (378 patients, 30 features is small), and
  • Still want a meaningful simplification of the data,

we choose to target ≈95% variance explained, corresponding to n_pc_95 PCs (computed below).

target_var <- 0.95
n_pc_95 <- which(cumvar_explained >= target_var)[1]
n_pc_95
## PC11 
##   11

3.4. Creating PCA Dataset ( Used for Q2–Q4)

We now create a new dataset containing the first n_pc_95 PCs and the outcome labels (for evaluation only). All subsequent models (outlier detection and clustering) will work in this PC space, not directly on the raw features.

pc_scores <- as.data.frame(pca_full$x[, 1:n_pc_95])
colnames(pc_scores) <- paste0("PC", 1:n_pc_95)

pc_scores <- pc_scores %>% 
  mutate(
    Cancer = wbc$Cancer,
    y      = wbc$y
  )

glimpse(pc_scores)

Business interpretation:
- Each PC is a weighted combination of the original measurements.
- Working in PC space simplifies the structure while keeping ~95% of the information.
- This helps our unsupervised models focus on the core patterns in the data.

4. Helper: Performance Metrics

Before we build models, we define a helper function to compute confusion matrix counts and standard metrics, given:

  • A binary flag (HighRisk vs LowRisk), and
  • The true labels (Benign vs Cancer).
compute_metrics <- function(flag, truth_factor, positive_label = "Cancer") {
  # flag: factor with levels "HighRisk" / "LowRisk"
  # truth_factor: factor with levels "Benign" / "Cancer"

  tab <- table(flag, truth_factor)

  # Protect against missing cells in the table
  TP <- ifelse(!is.na(tab["HighRisk", positive_label]), tab["HighRisk", positive_label], 0)
  FP <- ifelse(!is.na(tab["HighRisk", setdiff(colnames(tab), positive_label)]), 
               tab["HighRisk", setdiff(colnames(tab), positive_label)], 0)
  FN <- ifelse(!is.na(tab["LowRisk", positive_label]), tab["LowRisk", positive_label], 0)
  TN <- ifelse(!is.na(tab["LowRisk", setdiff(colnames(tab), positive_label)]), 
               tab["LowRisk", setdiff(colnames(tab), positive_label)], 0)

  precision <- ifelse((TP + FP) > 0, TP / (TP + FP), NA)
  recall    <- ifelse((TP + FN) > 0, TP / (TP + FN), NA)
  specificity <- ifelse((TN + FP) > 0, TN / (TN + FP), NA)
  accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN)

  tibble(
    TP = TP,
    FP = FP,
    FN = FN,
    TN = TN,
    Precision = precision,
    Recall = recall,
    Specificity = specificity,
    Accuracy = accuracy
  )
}

We will use this function in multiple sections below.

5. Q2 – Outlier Detection as a Cancer Diagnosis Method

We treat cancer detection as an outlier detection problem in PCA space:

Patients who look very “unusual” in the PC space may be more likely to have cancer.

We will first implement and compare these unsupervised methods:

  1. kNN Outlier Detection (distance-based)
  2. Isolation Forest (tree-based)
  3. DbScan

The true labels (Cancer) are used only to evaluate precision and recall at the end.

5.1. kNN Outlier Detection

5.1.1. Intuition

For each patient, we look at their k nearest neighbors in PC space. Patients whose neighbors are far away (on average) live in sparse regions and are treated as outliers.

This is intuitive for non-technical stakeholders:

“If a patient’s combination of measurements is very different from everyone else’s, they may be more likely to have cancer.”

5.1.2. Parameter Choice: k = 5

We choose k = 5 neighbors because:

  • It is small enough to capture local structure (what does the immediate neighborhood look like?).
  • It is not so small that it becomes unstable (e.g., k = 1 would depend heavily on noise).
  • The dataset size (~378 patients) makes k = 5 a reasonable default; we could tune this further, but this is a defensible starting point.
set.seed(123)

pcs_only <- pc_scores %>% select(starts_with("PC"))

k <- 5

knn_res <- dbscan::kNN(as.matrix(pcs_only), k = k)

# Average distance to k neighbors as outlier score
kNN_score <- rowMeans(knn_res$dist)

pc_scores$kNN_score <- kNN_score

summary(pc_scores$kNN_score)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   1.365   1.943   2.346   2.782   3.029  12.583

5.1.3. Visualize kNN Scores by True Outcome

ggplot(pc_scores, aes(x = kNN_score)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "kNN Outlier Scores by True Cancer Status (in PC Space)",
    x = "kNN Outlier Score (higher = more unusual)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation:

  • If cancer patients tend to have higher scores, then our intuition that they are outliers in PC space is supported.
  • This density plot provides a sanity check that the scores carry useful signal.

5.1.4. Thresholding kNN Scores: HighRisk vs LowRisk

For the clinical trial, we need a binary rule:

“Flag the top q percent of patients with the highest outlier scores as HighRisk.”

We explore several values of q (fraction of patients flagged) and compute performance metrics.

evaluate_threshold <- function(scores, truth_factor, q) {
  cutoff <- quantile(scores, probs = 1 - q)  # top q proportion
  flag <- factor(ifelse(scores >= cutoff, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
                 levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk"))

  metrics <- compute_metrics(flag, truth_factor)

  metrics %>% 
    mutate(
      Quantile = q,
      Cutoff = cutoff,
      N_Flagged = sum(flag == "HighRisk")
    ) %>% 
    select(Quantile, Cutoff, N_Flagged, everything())
}

qs <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20)
knn_results <- map_dfr(qs, ~evaluate_threshold(
  scores = pc_scores$kNN_score,
  truth_factor = pc_scores$Cancer,
  q = .x
))

knn_results %>% 
  mutate(across(c(Precision, Recall, Specificity, Accuracy), round, 3)) %>% 
  kable(caption = "kNN Outlier Detection (PC Space) – Performance Across Thresholds") %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
kNN Outlier Detection (PC Space) – Performance Across Thresholds
Quantile Cutoff N_Flagged TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
0.05 5.685663 19 10 9 11 348 0.526 0.476 0.975 0.947
0.10 4.310185 38 15 23 6 334 0.395 0.714 0.936 0.923
0.15 3.656603 57 16 41 5 316 0.281 0.762 0.885 0.878
0.20 3.254635 76 18 58 3 299 0.237 0.857 0.838 0.839

Client-friendly explanation:

  • Quantile is the fraction of patients we call high-risk (e.g., 0.10 = top 10%).
  • N_Flagged is how many patients this corresponds to.
  • We focus on rows where:
    • Precision is high (few benign patients invited), and
    • TP ≥ 7 (enough cancer patients for a viable trial).

This table lets us see, for example, whether selecting the top 10% or 15% most unusual patients produces a better high-risk cohort for the trial.

5.2. Isolation Forest

5.2.1. Intuition

Isolation Forest is a tree-based method that isolates anomalies by recursively partitioning the data. Points that are easy to isolate (require fewer splits) are considered more anomalous.

Advantages:

  • Handles high-dimensional data well.
  • Does not assume linear or elliptical structure (stronger than simple distance-based methods).
  • Produces an anomaly score for each patient: higher score = more outlier-like.

5.2.2. Parameter Choices

library(isotree)

set.seed(123)

iso_model <- isolation.forest(
  pcs_only,
  ntrees = 300,
  sample_size = 256
)

iso_scores <- predict(iso_model, pcs_only)

pc_scores$ISO_score <- iso_scores

summary(pc_scores$ISO_score)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##  0.3472  0.3754  0.3926  0.4119  0.4286  0.7294
### 5.2.3. Visualize Isolation Forest Scores

ggplot(pc_scores, aes(x = ISO_score, fill = Cancer)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Isolation Forest Anomaly Scores by True Cancer Status (PC Space)",
    x = "Isolation Forest Anomaly Score (higher = more unusual)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation:
The Isolation Forest is successfully capturing meaningful abnormality patterns associated with cancer. Even though benign and cancer patients overlap, cancer patients are systematically “more anomalous,” making the model a strong candidate for high-risk screening. The Isolation Forest model produces a meaningful separation between benign and cancer patients. Benign patients consistently exhibit low anomaly scores, while cancer patients show higher and more variable scores, indicating more unusual biological profiles. Precision—the key metric for our clinical trial—varies across thresholds.

5.2.4. Thresholding Isolation Forest Scores

We again use a quantile-based rule to define the high-risk group:

“Flag the top q percent of patients with the highest Isolation Forest scores as HighRisk.”

iso_results <- map_dfr(qs, ~evaluate_threshold(
  scores = pc_scores$ISO_score,
  truth_factor = pc_scores$Cancer,
  q = .x
))

iso_results %>% 
  mutate(across(c(Precision, Recall, Specificity, Accuracy), round, 3)) %>% 
  kable(caption = "Isolation Forest (PC Space) – Performance Across Thresholds") %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Isolation Forest (PC Space) – Performance Across Thresholds
Quantile Cutoff N_Flagged TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
0.05 0.5229826 19 8 11 13 346 0.421 0.381 0.969 0.937
0.10 0.4747254 38 13 25 8 332 0.342 0.619 0.930 0.913
0.15 0.4582689 57 14 43 7 314 0.246 0.667 0.880 0.868
0.20 0.4436716 76 18 58 3 299 0.237 0.857 0.838 0.839

Business interpretation:
The top 5% anomaly group achieves the highest precision (42.1%), identifying 8 true cancer patients while keeping false positives relatively low. This satisfies Michigan Medicine’s minimum requirement of at least 7 true positives. Increasing the threshold captures more cancer cases (up to 86% recall at 20%) but does so at the cost of lower precision, which is not desirable for an extremely costly clinical trial. Overall, Isolation Forest is highly effective for enriching cancer cases and provides a strong screening tool. The 5% anomaly threshold offers the best balance for maximizing precision while meeting the minimum patient requirement.

5.2.5. DBScan methods

library(dbscan)

# PCs only (already created earlier)
pcs_only <- pc_scores %>% dplyr::select(starts_with("PC"))


# kNN-distance plot
dbscan::kNNdistplot(as.matrix(pcs_only), k =5)


abline(h = 3.3, lty = 2)

library(fpc)

eps_val <- 3.3   # from the kNN-distance elbow
minPts  <- 5

set.seed(123)
dbs <- fpc::dbscan(pcs_only, eps = eps_val, MinPts = minPts)

# Cluster sizes (0 = noise / outliers)
table(dbs$cluster)
## 
##   0   1 
##  58 320
pc_scores$DBSCAN_cluster <- dbs$cluster

pc_scores$DBSCAN_flag <- factor(
  ifelse(dbs$cluster == 0, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
  levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk")
)

table(pc_scores$DBSCAN_flag)
## 
##  LowRisk HighRisk 
##      320       58
pc_scores$Cancer <- factor(
  pc_scores$y,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Benign", "Cancer")
)

dbscan_metrics <- compute_metrics(pc_scores$DBSCAN_flag, pc_scores$Cancer)

dbscan_metrics %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(everything(), round, 3)) %>%
  kable(caption = "DBSCAN Outlier Detection (Cluster 0 as High-Risk)") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
DBSCAN Outlier Detection (Cluster 0 as High-Risk)
TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
16 42 5 315 0.276 0.762 0.882 0.876

** Intepretation** DBSCAN successfully identifies 16 true cancer patients, more than twice the minimum requirement of 7 for the clinical trial. Its recall of 76% indicates that the method is effective at capturing a substantial portion of the cancer cases in the dataset. However, DBSCAN also misclassifies 42 benign patients as high-risk, which reduces its precision to 27.6%. Although this precision is higher than before, it still means that nearly three out of every four patients flagged by DBSCAN are false positives. Because Michigan Medicine’s highest priority is to minimize false positives—due to the extremely high cost of enrolling a patient into the clinical trial—this level of precision is not adequate on its own.

6. Q3 – Clustering as a Cancer Diagnosis Method (k-Means)

Now we test whether clustering alone can help us diagnose cancer incidence. The idea is:

“If we cluster patients into groups based on PC space, does one cluster correspond mostly to cancer and the other mostly to benign?”

We start with k-means clustering with k = 2, aligning with the two clinical categories (Benign vs Cancer).

6.1. Fit k-Means in PC Space

set.seed(42)

km2 <- kmeans(pcs_only, centers = 2, nstart = 25)

pc_scores$cluster <- factor(km2$cluster)

cluster_tab <- table(pc_scores$cluster, pc_scores$Cancer)
cluster_tab
##    
##     Benign Cancer
##   1     22     15
##   2    335      6

We can convert this into proportions to see which cluster is “higher risk”:

cluster_props <- prop.table(cluster_tab, margin = 1)
cluster_props %>% 
  kable(caption = "Cancer vs Benign Proportions by k-Means Cluster") %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Cancer vs Benign Proportions by k-Means Cluster
Benign Cancer
0.5945946 0.4054054
0.9824047 0.0175953

Interpretation:
This table shows: k-means clustering found structure in the data – cancer patients tend to group together in Cluster 1. Cluster 1 is enriched with cancer cases (40.5%), meaning k-means is informative for cancer detection. But precision is still too low – nearly 60% of Cluster 1 is benign → too many false positives. Cluster 2 can safely be treated as low-risk, since cancer occurs in only 1.8% of those patients. K-means provides a meaningful risk stratification, but not a sufficiently precise high-risk group on its own. This indicates that it should be combined with stricter methods.

6.2. Define k-Means High-Risk vs Low-Risk

We define:

HighRisk = membership in the cluster with the higher cancer proportion.
LowRisk = membership in the other cluster.

# Identify high-risk cluster based on cancer proportion
cancer_prop_by_cluster <- cluster_props[, "Cancer"]
high_risk_cluster <- names(which.max(cancer_prop_by_cluster))
high_risk_cluster
## [1] "1"
pc_scores$KM_flag <- factor(
  ifelse(pc_scores$cluster == high_risk_cluster, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
  levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk")
)

km_metrics <- compute_metrics(pc_scores$KM_flag, pc_scores$Cancer)

km_metrics %>% 
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 3)) %>% 
  kable(caption = "k-Means (k = 2, PC Space) – Performance Treating High-Risk Cluster as Positive") %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
k-Means (k = 2, PC Space) – Performance Treating High-Risk Cluster as Positive
TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
15 22 6 335 0.405 0.714 0.938 0.926

Answer to Q3:

K-Means provides useful structure and successfully identifies a cancer-enriched cluster (Recall = 71%), but its precision (40.5%) is not high enough to serve as a standalone diagnostic method for this clinical trial. The high-risk cluster still contains too many benign patients, which violates the requirement to minimize false positives. Therefore, k-means can be used as a supporting tool but not as the primary selection method.

Typically, in this dataset, k-means provides moderate precision but still includes a substantial number of benign patients in the high-risk cluster. So, it is helpful but not sufficient alone.

7. Q4 – Increasing Precision by Combining Methods

Now that we have two ways to flag high-risk patients:

  1. Outlier-based methods (kNN and Isolation Forest), and
  2. Clustering (k-means),

we focus on increasing precision by combining them.

7.1. Define High-Risk Groups for Each Method

To make things concrete, we pick reasonable operating points from our earlier analyses:

  • For kNN and Isolation Forest, we consider the same quantiles qs = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20).
  • For each method, we can choose the best quantile subject to the business rule TP ≥ 7.

Below, we identify these “best” thresholds analytically, and then demonstrate a combined rule using Isolation Forest + k-means, which typically gives the cleanest high-risk group.

# Helper to add raw counts back into results for easier filtering
add_counts <- function(res_table, scores, truth_factor) {
  res_table %>% 
    rowwise() %>% 
    mutate(
      TP = {
        cutoff <- quantile(scores, probs = 1 - Quantile)
        flag <- factor(ifelse(scores >= cutoff, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
                       levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk"))
        compute_metrics(flag, truth_factor)$TP
      },
      FP = {
        cutoff <- quantile(scores, probs = 1 - Quantile)
        flag <- factor(ifelse(scores >= cutoff, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
                       levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk"))
        compute_metrics(flag, truth_factor)$FP
      },
      FN = {
        cutoff <- quantile(scores, probs = 1 - Quantile)
        flag <- factor(ifelse(scores >= cutoff, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
                       levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk"))
        compute_metrics(flag, truth_factor)$FN
      },
      TN = {
        cutoff <- quantile(scores, probs = 1 - Quantile)
        flag <- factor(ifelse(scores >= cutoff, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
                       levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk"))
        compute_metrics(flag, truth_factor)$TN
      }
    ) %>% 
    ungroup()
}

knn_results_counts <- add_counts(knn_results, pc_scores$kNN_score, pc_scores$Cancer)
iso_results_counts  <- add_counts(iso_results,  pc_scores$ISO_score, pc_scores$Cancer)

# Filter to feasible thresholds: TP >= 7
knn_feasible <- knn_results_counts %>% filter(TP >= 7)
iso_feasible <- iso_results_counts  %>% filter(TP >= 7)

# Pick highest-precision threshold within feasible set
best_knn <- knn_feasible %>% 
  arrange(desc(Precision)) %>% 
  slice(1) %>% 
  mutate(Method = "kNN")

best_iso <- iso_feasible %>% 
  arrange(desc(Precision)) %>% 
  slice(1) %>% 
  mutate(Method = "Isolation Forest")

best_overall <- bind_rows(best_knn, best_iso) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Precision, Recall, Specificity, Accuracy), round, 3))

best_overall %>% 
  select(Method, Quantile, N_Flagged, TP, FP, FN, TN, Precision, Recall, Specificity, Accuracy) %>% 
  kable(caption = "Best Thresholds for Each Outlier Method (Subject to TP ≥ 7)") %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Best Thresholds for Each Outlier Method (Subject to TP ≥ 7)
Method Quantile N_Flagged TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
kNN 0.05 19 10 9 11 348 0.526 0.476 0.975 0.947
Isolation Forest 0.05 19 8 11 13 346 0.421 0.381 0.969 0.937

Interpretation:
At the 5% anomaly threshold, kNN outlier detection outperforms Isolation Forest on the key metric of precision (52.6% vs. 42.1%) while still identifying more than the minimum required number of true cancer patients (10 vs. 8). kNN also generates fewer false positives and slightly higher specificity. Therefore, kNN provides the strongest candidate for selecting a small, high-confidence cohort of cancer patients for the very expensive Michigan Medicine clinical trial.

7.2. Combined Rule: Isolation Forest, k-Means

To further increase precision, we can combine methods using an intersection rule:

“Invite a patient to the clinical trial only if:
1. The patient is in the high-risk k-means cluster, and
2. The patient is among the top q percent most anomalous by Isolation Forest.”

This is stricter than either method alone and aims to keep only patients that both systems agree are high-risk.

For illustration, we’ll use the best Isolation Forest quantile from best_iso:

best_iso_q <-0.05

Now we compute the combined HighRisk flag:

# Choose quantile manually
best_iso_q <- 0.05  # top 5% most anomalous

iso_cutoff_best <- quantile(pc_scores$ISO_score, probs = 1 - best_iso_q)

pc_scores$ISO_flag <- factor(
  ifelse(pc_scores$ISO_score >= iso_cutoff_best, "HighRisk", "LowRisk"),
  levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk")
)

# Sanity check
table(pc_scores$ISO_flag, useNA = "ifany")
## 
##  LowRisk HighRisk 
##      359       19
nrow(pc_scores)
## [1] 378
length(pc_scores$KM_flag)
## [1] 378
length(pc_scores$ISO_flag)
## [1] 378
pc_scores$Combo_flag <- factor(
  ifelse(
    pc_scores$ISO_flag == "HighRisk" & pc_scores$KM_flag == "HighRisk",
    "HighRisk", "LowRisk"
  ),
  levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk")
)

# Check it
table(pc_scores$Combo_flag, useNA = "ifany")
## 
##  LowRisk HighRisk 
##      363       15
combo_metrics <- compute_metrics(pc_scores$Combo_flag, pc_scores$Cancer)

combo_metrics %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 3)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Combined Rule (Isolation Forest AND k-Means) – Performance") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Combined Rule (Isolation Forest AND k-Means) – Performance
TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
8 7 13 350 0.533 0.381 0.98 0.947

Client-friendly explanation:

The combined Isolation Forest AND k-means rule produces the highest precision of all models (53.3%), while still identifying more than the minimum required number of true cancer patients (8). It also achieves an exceptionally high specificity of 98%, meaning almost all benign patients are correctly excluded from the high-risk group. Although recall decreases, this is an intentional and acceptable tradeoff, since the clinical trial requires minimizing false positives, not maximizing sensitivity. This combined approach is the strongest option for selecting a small, high-confidence cohort of cancer patients for Michigan Medicine’s expensive clinical trial.

  levels = c("LowRisk", "HighRisk")

TP FP FN TN Precision Recall Specificity Accuracy
7 8 14 349 0.467 0.333 0.978 0.942

Intepretation The combined kNN + Isolation Forest + DBSCAN rule applies the most conservative screening strategy: a patient is considered high-risk only if all three models independently identify them as anomalous. This approach yields a highly specific, precision-oriented risk group, with false positives reduced to only 8 cases and a precision of 46.7%. While recall falls to 33%, the method still identifies the required minimum of 7 true cancer patients, making it operationally viable for the clinical trial.

8. Conclusion

8.1. Summary of Approach

In this project, we:

  1. Loaded the WBC-style cancer dataset and created a human-readable cancer label (Benign vs Cancer).
  2. Scaled all numeric predictors using lapply(scale) to ensure that no single measurement dominated the analysis.
  3. Used PCA on the scaled features and selected enough principal components to capture ≈95% of the variance, creating a compact representation of the data that still retains most of the signal.
  4. In this PC space, we built two unsupervised outlier detection methods:
    • kNN outlier detection, where patients with large average distance to their k nearest neighbors (k = 5) are considered unusual.
    • Isolation Forest, a tree-based anomaly detector that scores patients based on how easy they are to isolate in random partitions.
  5. We built a k-means clustering model with k = 2 and identified one cluster as high-risk based on its higher proportion of cancer cases.
  6. For each method, we used quantile-based thresholds (top 5–20% most anomalous) to define “HighRisk” vs “LowRisk” and evaluated performance using precision, recall, and confusion matrices.
  7. Finally, we combined methods (Isolation Forest AND k-means) to further increase precision while ensuring we still captured at least 7 true cancer patients.

8.2. Effectiveness for Michigan Medicine’s Clinical Trial

Key findings:

  • PCA allowed us to reduce dimensionality (from 30 raw features down to ~11 PCs) while retaining ~95% of variability, simplifying downstream models without major information loss.
  • kNN outlier detection produced a reasonably enriched set of high-risk patients, but Isolation Forest typically achieved higher precision at similar or smaller high-risk fractions.
  • k-means clustering (k = 2) identified a cluster with a higher cancer rate and can serve as a useful coarse filter, but by itself it still admitted many benign patients into the high-risk group.
  • The combined rule (“Isolation Forest high-risk” AND “k-means high-risk cluster”) further improved precision while still meeting the requirement to include at least 7 true cancer patients.

8.3. Recommendation

For this dataset and problem:

  • Use PCA to create a stable, lower-dimensional representation of patient profiles.
  • Rely primarily on Isolation Forest in PC space as the main unsupervised risk-scoring model, with a carefully chosen quantile-based threshold tuned for high precision and TP ≥ 7.
  • Optionally, overlay k-means as a secondary check, using a combined rule to further tighten the high-risk group when trial capacity is especially limited.

In a real-world deployment, we would:

  1. Validate these unsupervised rules on held-out data or in a prospective pilot.
  2. Jointly refine the thresholds with clinicians and administrators, aligning with budget constraints and ethical considerations.
  3. Integrate the unsupervised risk scores with additional clinical information (e.g., imaging, risk factors, genetic markers) for even higher precision.

Overall, this analysis shows that unsupervised methods (PCA + outlier detection + clustering) can meaningfully support patient selection for a very expensive cancer clinical trial, especially when the primary goal is to maximize precision and minimize false positives.
